screens.title: ASBRs and External Routes in OSPF
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will learn what an Autonomous System Boundary Router, or ASBR, does in an OSPF network and why correct redistribution matters. An ASBR is the gateway that imports routes learned by static configuration, other IGPs, or BGP into an OSPF autonomous system. You will learn the LSA mechanisms used to carry those routes — the Type 5 external LSA and the Type 7 NSSA external LSA — and how Junos controls metric and metric-type when redistributing. We will show concrete Junos configuration examples for creating a redistribution policy and applying it to OSPF, including how to set the seed metric and choose between E1 and E2. You will also see practical caveats: stub areas cannot contain an ASBR, NSSAs use Type 7 with ABR translation, and redistribution loops are a common misconfiguration if tagging or filters are not used. By the end you will be able to explain when to prefer E1 versus E2, create a Junos export policy for static routes, and verify external LSAs and learned external routes on internal routers.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

ASBR role and redistribution essentials

Understand how external networks enter OSPF, which LSAs carry them, and how metric type changes path selection.

Estimated audio: 1m 20s
In this lesson

ASBR function, Type 5/7 LSAs, E1 vs E2, Junos redistribution policy and verification.

Coming up

Live-coding Junos examples and step-by-step verification using show commands.

Concept map
ASBR → Redistribute → Type 5 / Type 7 → E1 / E2
ASBR

Gateway that injects non-OSPF routes into the OSPF domain.

LSA Types

Type 5 floods the AS; Type 7 is used inside NSSA and translated at the ABR.

Metrics

E2 uses the seed metric only; E1 adds internal cost to the ASBR for shortest-path selection.

Quick topics

Explore Key Topics

ASBR role
How external routes are made visible to OSPF routers.
E1 vs E2
When to add internal cost and when to rely on a seed metric.
NSSA behavior
Type 7 LSAs and ABR translation to Type 5 for backbone propagation.
Why this matters

Redistribution decisions shape reachability and path selection across an OSPF domain. Picking the wrong metric type or failing to filter redistributed routes can cause suboptimal paths or routing loops. This chapter prepares you to configure Junos ASBRs safely and verify the results from internal routers.

screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map directly to the practical tasks an engineer will perform when working with ASBRs and external routes. First, you will be able to identify the role and characteristics of an ASBR and explain why it is required to import non-OSPF networks into an OSPF autonomous system. Second, you will understand route redistribution mechanics: how Junos selects routes via a policy, how exported routes are converted into LSAs, and the commands used for verification. Third, you will learn to distinguish between Type 5 and Type 7 LSAs and explain how an NSSA ABR translates Type 7 into Type 5 for backbone distribution. Finally, you will be able to choose and configure external route types, E1 or E2, based on whether internal OSPF cost should influence path selection, and apply that choice in a Junos export statement. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you know when you are ready to practice in a lab or on real devices.

screens.title: What is an ASBR?
screens.narratorSegment: An ASBR is a router that connects an OSPF autonomous system to networks outside OSPF and injects those external routes into the OSPF domain. Think of the ASBR as a customs gate between two countries: it informs the OSPF world about routes that exist outside, and it marks information so internal routers can reach those networks. Concretely, an ASBR might redistribute static routes, routes learned from BGP, or routes from another IGP. Without an ASBR performing redistribution, internal OSPF routers would remain unaware of external prefixes. A common real example is a network edge router that learns internet prefixes via BGP and redistributes selected prefixes into OSPF so internal routers can forward traffic to the edge. A common misconception is believing any router connected to an external network becomes an ASBR automatically; in practice the router is only an ASBR when you configure redistribution into OSPF. Another pitfall is placing an ASBR inside a stub or totally stubby area; that violates OSPF rules because those area types block Type 5 LSAs which advertise external routes. Key takeaway: ASBRs enable reachability to external networks by converting non-OSPF routes into OSPF external LSAs, and correct policy and placement are essential to avoid unexpected reachability or LSA filtering issues.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › What is an ASBR?
Definition

Autonomous System Boundary Router

A router that connects an OSPF domain to external routing sources and redistributes routes into OSPF so internal routers can reach them.

Analogy

Like a customs gate: it reports external networks and enforces which ones are allowed into OSPF.

Misconception

Connected to an external link does not auto-make a router an ASBR; explicit redistribution makes it one.

Concrete example

An edge router learns internet prefixes via BGP and you choose to redistribute selected prefixes into OSPF so internal routers can forward traffic toward the edge without running BGP everywhere.

Why it matters

Proper redistribution controls reachability and prevents unstable routing if filters or tags are missing.

Key takeaway

Only configure redistribution where you want OSPF to learn external prefixes and protect against loops with tagging and policies.

screens.title: Type 5 and Type 7 LSAs
screens.narratorSegment: When an ASBR redistributes an external network into OSPF it must advertise that network in a Link-State Advertisement designed for external prefixes. The standard LSA for redistributed routes is the Type 5 External LSA. A Type 5 LSA describes a single external prefix and the originating ASBR; Type 5 LSAs are flooded to all areas in the autonomous system that accept them, except stub and totally stubby areas which block Type 5. A special case exists for Not-So-Totally Stubby Areas: ASBRs inside an NSSA generate Type 7 NSSA External LSAs. Those Type 7 LSAs are flooded only within the NSSA. When a Type 7 reaches the NSSA's ABR, the ABR translates it into a Type 5 LSA so the backbone and other areas can learn the external prefix. This translation supports the NSSA design goal: allow limited external injection while still preventing Type 5s from flooding into the NSSA from outside. A common misconception is that Type 7 LSAs alone reach the backbone; in reality the ABR must perform translation for external knowledge to leave the NSSA. Remember to verify with show ospf database external and show ospf database nssa to confirm which LSA types are present.

keyIdea.title: LSA rule
keyIdea.text: Use Type 5 for general external LSAs; use Type 7 for NSSA internal external LSAs that ABRs translate to Type 5 for backbone propagation.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Type 5 & Type 7 LSAs
Concept

Type 5 vs Type 7

Type 5 LSAs advertise external prefixes throughout the OSPF autonomous system. Type 7 LSAs are generated inside an NSSA and are translated by the ABR into Type 5 for backbone distribution.

Type 5
  • Flooded to areas that accept externals (not stub/TSA)
  • Originated by an ASBR exporting routes
Type 7
  • Used inside NSSA for redistributed prefixes
  • Translated by ABR into Type 5 before entering Area 0
Example scenario

If an ASBR in an NSSA redistributes a static route 172.16.10.0/24, it creates a Type 7 LSA inside that NSSA. When that LSA reaches the ABR, the ABR converts it to a Type 5 LSA so Area 0 and other non-NSSA areas can learn the external prefix.

Key Takeaway

NSSAs allow local redistribution via Type 7 while preventing direct Type 5 flooding into the area; ABR translation is required for backbone visibility.

screens.title: E2 versus E1 External Routes
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between External Type 2 and External Type 1 routes changes how OSPF evaluates the cost to reach an external destination. E2 is the default for redistributed routes. With E2, routers use the external seed metric advertised by the ASBR; they do not add the internal OSPF cost to reach the ASBR. The practical consequence is that all routers see the same total cost to reach that external destination, so internal topology distance does not change selection. E2 is useful when the advertised external metric alone reflects the desired preference, or when a consistent cost across the domain is acceptable. By contrast, E1 adds the internal OSPF cost to the ASBR to the external seed metric. This means routers closer to an ASBR will see a lower total cost and may prefer that ASBR when multiple ASBRs advertise the same prefix. E1 is appropriate when you want true shortest-path routing to external destinations based on internal topology. A common mistake is leaving metric-type at the default E2 when multiple ASBRs exist, which can result in non-optimal forwarding. Always consider whether internal cost should influence ASBR selection before choosing the metric type.

keyIdea.title: Metric choice
keyIdea.text: E2 uses seed metric only; E1 adds internal cost to ASBR so OSPF picks the nearest ASBR by cost.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › E2 vs E1
External Type 2 (E2)

Default: seed metric only

With E2, the internal OSPF cost to reach the ASBR is not added. All routers see the advertised external metric as the total cost. Use this when a consistent external cost is desired.

When to use
  • Single ASBR environments or when external metric determines preference.
  • Simpler, predictable external cost across domain.
External Type 1 (E1)

Seed metric plus internal cost

E1 adds the internal cost to the ASBR to the external seed metric, letting OSPF choose the closest ASBR by total cost when multiple ASBRs advertise the same prefix.

When to use
  • Multiple ASBRs announcing the same external prefixes where closest ASBR should be preferred.
  • When internal topology should influence external path selection.
Misconception

Default E2 always gives optimal results — not true when multiple ASBRs exist and internal cost matters.

Pro tip

When changing metric-type, test with show route protocol ospf on an internal router to confirm expected cost behavior.

Check

If two ASBRs advertise the same prefix with E2, tie-breaking may rely on router ID; E1 explicitly favors the nearer ASBR.

screens.title: Junos Redistribution Example — Policy and Export
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a Junos configuration pattern to redistribute static routes into OSPF with a controlled metric and metric-type. First, create a policy-statement that matches protocol static and accepts those routes. This policy acts as the filter determining exactly which routes are eligible for export. Next, apply that policy to OSPF with an export statement; you can set metric and metric-type there or within the policy depending on your design. In the provided example we use a policy named REDISTRIBUTE_STATIC and then apply it with set protocols ospf export REDISTRIBUTE_STATIC and set protocols ospf export REDISTRIBUTE_STATIC metric 200 metric-type 1 for E1 behavior. A concrete example: configure a static route for 172.16.10.0/24 on the ASBR, write the policy to match static, and export with metric-type 1 so internal cost is added. A common mistake is forgetting the export statement after creating the policy — the policy exists but isn't applied, so no routes are redistributed. Another pitfall is setting an inappropriate seed metric; choose values consistently across ASBRs when you want predictable comparisons. After configuration, verify with show ospf database external on the ASBR and show route protocol ospf on an internal router to confirm type and metric.

Next, apply that policy to OSPF with an export statement; you can set metric and metric-type there or within the policy depending on your design. After configuration, verify with show ospf database external on the ASBR and show route protocol ospf on an internal router to confirm type and metric.

keyIdea.title: Junos pattern
keyIdea.text: Create a routing-policy to match routes and apply it with protocols ospf export, specifying metric and metric-type for redistribution.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Junos Redistribution Example
Config template
# Define a policy to select static routes
set policy-options policy-statement REDISTRIBUTE_STATIC term 1 from protocol static
set policy-options policy-statement REDISTRIBUTE_STATIC term 1 then accept

# Apply the policy to OSPF and specify metric and metric-type
set protocols ospf export REDISTRIBUTE_STATIC
set protocols ospf export REDISTRIBUTE_STATIC metric 200 metric-type 1

# Interface and area examples
set interfaces ge-0/0/0 unit 0 family inet address 10.0.0.1/24
set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface ge-0/0/0.0
Concrete example

Configure static 172.16.10.0/24 on R1, create REDISTRIBUTE_STATIC to match protocol static, and export with metric 200 metric-type 1 so internal cost is added.

Common mistake

Creating a policy but not applying it via set protocols ospf export — no redistribution will occur.

Verification
On the ASBR: show ospf database external — confirm Type 5 LSA for redistributed prefix.
On internal router: show route protocol ospf — confirm the external route, metric, and whether it shows Ext1 or Ext2.
Key Takeaway

Policies control what is redistributed; export with metric and metric-type controls how OSPF treats that external route.

screens.title: Step-by-step Redistribution Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: When configuring redistribution on an ASBR follow a clear workflow to avoid mistakes. Step one: identify and verify the external routes you intend to redistribute, for example a static route or routes learned from BGP. Step two: author a routing-policy that precisely matches only those routes; avoid overly broad terms that pick up unintended prefixes. Step three: apply the policy to OSPF with an export statement and choose metric and metric-type according to design — metric-type 2 if seed metric should dominate, metric-type 1 if internal cost should influence selection. Step four: verify on the ASBR that the appropriate external LSAs are generated using show ospf database external or show ospf database nssa for NSSA scenarios. Step five: check internal routers with show route protocol ospf to confirm the external route exists and the metric and type match expectations. Finally, step six: monitor for redistribution loops and unexpected reachability changes; if you redistribute bi-directionally, use route tagging and filters to prevent re-injection into the source protocol. Following this process helps ensure predictable, safe redistribution. Step-by-step Redistribution Workflow means identify → policy → export with metric/metric-type → verify lsas → verify internal routes → prevent loops with tags/filters.. In practical terms, from matching routes to verification on internal routers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Redistribution Workflow
Six steps
1
Identify external routes
Locate the static or external prefixes you will redistribute and confirm next-hops.
2
Create routing-policy
Match by protocol or prefix and accept only intended routes to avoid accidental exports.
3
Apply export with metric
Use set protocols ospf export and set metric/metric-type to control E1/E2 behavior.
4
Verify LSAs on ASBR
Run show ospf database external or show ospf database nssa to confirm correct LSA type.
5
Confirm internal routing
On an internal router run show route protocol ospf to check metric and external type.
6
Prevent loops
Use route tags and filters when redistributing bi-directionally to avoid re-injection into the source protocol.
Example check

After export, expect a Type 5 for normal AS or Type 7 for NSSA; the internal router should list the route under OSPF with the chosen external type and metric.

Key Takeaway

A disciplined six-step process reduces configuration errors and helps you validate expected behavior quickly.

screens.title: NSSA ABR Translation Mechanics
screens.narratorSegment: An NSSA allows limited external route injection while preventing Type 5 LSAs from entering the area from outside. When an ASBR inside an NSSA redistributes an external prefix, it generates a Type 7 LSA which is flooded only within the NSSA. The crucial role of the Area Border Router here is translation. When the ABR receives a Type 7 LSA from the NSSA, it converts that LSA into a Type 5 External LSA for distribution into Area 0 and the rest of the autonomous system. This ensures the external route becomes visible to internal routers outside the NSSA while preserving the NSSA's filtering on incoming Type 5 LSAs. Verification steps include checking the ABR's database for both Type 7 and translated Type 5 LSAs. A potential misconception is assuming translation loses the seed metric or type; the ABR preserves the external metric and the chosen metric-type semantics when translating. When designing networks, remember NSSA is useful when you need a local ASBR but do not want Type 5 LSAs to flood into that area; ABR translation bridges local injection with global visibility in a controlled way.

When the ABR receives a Type 7 LSA from the NSSA, it converts that LSA into a Type 5 External LSA for distribution into Area 0 and the rest of the autonomous system. This ensures the external route becomes visible to internal routers outside the NSSA while preserving the NSSA's filtering on incoming Type 5 LSAs. A potential misconception is assuming translation loses the seed metric or type; the ABR preserves the external metric and the chosen metric-type semantics when translating. When designing networks, remember NSSA is useful when you need a local ASBR but do not want Type 5 LSAs to flood into that area; ABR translation bridges local injection with global visibility in a controlled way.

keyIdea.title: Translation role
keyIdea.text: ABRs translate Type 7 LSAs from NSSAs to Type 5 LSAs so external prefixes become visible to the backbone and other areas.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › NSSA ABR Translation
How it works

An ASBR inside an NSSA generates Type 7 LSAs for redistributed routes. The ABR converts those Type 7 LSAs into Type 5 LSAs before flooding them into Area 0 and other areas that accept external LSAs.

What to verify

On the ASBR: show ospf database nssa to confirm Type 7. On the ABR: show ospf database external to confirm translated Type 5.

Design note

Use NSSA when you need local redistribution but also want to avoid incoming Type 5 LSAs in that area.

Concrete scenario

R1 in NSSA redistributes a static route, creates Type 7. The ABR converts it to Type 5 and floods Area 0 so R2 in Area 0 learns the external prefix.

Key Takeaway

NSSA lets you redistribute locally while ABR translation ensures backbone visibility when needed.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Hands-on: R1 & R2
R1 (ASBR) example
# Interfaces and OSPF area
set interfaces ge-0/0/0 unit 0 family inet address 10.0.0.1/24
set interfaces lo0 unit 0 family inet address 192.168.0.1/32
set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface ge-0/0/0.0
set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface lo0.0 passive

# Static route to redistribute
set routing-options static route 172.16.10.0/24 next-hop 10.0.0.254

# Policy to match static routes
set policy-options policy-statement REDISTRIBUTE_STATIC from protocol static
set policy-options policy-statement REDISTRIBUTE_STATIC then accept

# Apply export with metric and metric-type (E1)
set protocols ospf export REDISTRIBUTE_STATIC
set protocols ospf export REDISTRIBUTE_STATIC metric 200 metric-type 1
R2 (Internal)
# R2 minimal config
set interfaces ge-0/0/0 unit 0 family inet address 10.0.0.2/24
set interfaces lo0 unit 0 family inet address 192.168.0.2/32
set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface ge-0/0/0.0
set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface lo0.0 passive

# Verification: on R2
# show route protocol ospf  -> expect 172.16.10.0/24 as Ext1 with metric 200 (+ internal cost if E1)
Key Takeaway

Follow the example to confirm how metric-type affects what internal routers see, and re-run verification after changes.

screens.title: Avoiding Redistribution Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: While redistribution is powerful, several common mistakes can cause outages or suboptimal routing. First, an incorrect routing-policy may either leak unintended routes into OSPF or fail to export routes you need. Always test policies locally before applying to production. Second, selecting the wrong metric or metric-type can lead to poor path selection. For example, leaving default E2 in a multi-ASBR environment can cause routers to ignore internal distance and choose suboptimal forwarding paths. Third, redistribution loops occur when routes are redistributed in both directions without tagging or filtering; route tags prevent re-injection into the source protocol and are essential in complex designs. Fourth, placing an ASBR inside a stub or totally stubby area violates OSPF rules because these areas block Type 5 LSAs; an NSSA is the correct choice if you need a local ASBR. Finally, forgetting to apply the export statement after creating a policy is a simple but frequent operational error. Use the verification commands described earlier to confirm LSA types and routing table entries to catch these mistakes early. Avoiding Redistribution Pitfalls means use precise policies, choose metric-type intentionally, tag routes to avoid loops, and place asbrs only where lsas are accepted or use nssa appropriately.. In practical terms, policy mistakes, metric errors, and redistribution loops. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Redistribution Pitfalls
Common pitfalls
  • Incorrect or missing policy: Too broad or not applied; verify policy and export statement.
  • Wrong metric-type: Default E2 may hide internal cost and cause non-optimal ASBR selection when multiples exist.
  • Redistribution loops: Bi-directional redistribution without tags can re-inject routes back into the source protocol.
  • ASBR placement in stub areas: Stub and totally stubby areas cannot contain ASBRs because Type 5 LSAs are blocked.
Prevention checklist
  1. Create precise routing-policy to match only intended routes.
  2. Use metric tagging and consistent seed metrics across ASBRs when required.
  3. Apply route tags and filters for multi-protocol redistribution to prevent loops.
Watch out

Simple omissions like forgetting to apply the export policy are frequent and easy to test for during verification steps.

screens.title: Verification Commands and What to Expect
screens.narratorSegment: Verification is essential after configuring redistribution. Start on the ASBR by confirming OSPF adjacencies with show ospf neighbor; if adjacencies are missing, external LSAs will not propagate correctly. Next, confirm the static or external route is present in the routing table with show route and the specific prefix. Then inspect the OSPF database on the ASBR with show ospf database external to find Type 5 LSAs, or show ospf database nssa to see Type 7 LSAs if working inside an NSSA. On the ABR verify the translation by checking for translated Type 5 entries. Finally, on an internal router run show route protocol ospf; you should see the redistributed prefix with a protocol of OSPF and an external type of Ext1 or Ext2 matching your configuration. If metrics are unexpected, re-check the metric/metric-type on the export statement or the policy. These verification steps let you confirm both LSA generation and the behavior seen by downstream routers. A quick test after changes helps catch policy misconfigurations or unintended route leaks before they affect production traffic. Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Verification Commands
Common commands
show ospf neighbor
show route 172.16.10.0/24
show ospf database external
show ospf database nssa
show route protocol ospf
On ASBR: Expect the static route in the routing table and a Type 5 (or Type 7 for NSSA) in the OSPF database.
On ABR: Confirm translation from Type 7 to Type 5 for NSSA-sourced externals.
On internal router: Expect the prefix under OSPF with Ext1 or Ext2 depending on metric-type.
Diagnostic tips
  • If no external LSA appears, check the export policy and whether it is applied.
  • If metrics differ, check metric and metric-type in the export stanza and any policy-set attributes.
  • To trace loops, inspect route tags and history of redistributions between protocols.
Key Takeaway

Use the listed show commands to confirm both LSA presence and how downstream routers learn the external prefix; verification ensures correct behavior before traffic relies on redistributed routes.

screens.title: Design Decision: When to Use E1 or E2
screens.narratorSegment: Consider a network where two ASBRs redistribute the same external prefixes into Area 0. The design requirement is that internal routers should prefer the ASBR that is topologically closest in OSPF cost. Which external type should you configure and why? The correct design choice is External Type 1 because E1 adds the internal OSPF cost to the ASBR to the external seed metric. This allows routers nearer to a particular ASBR to see a lower total cost and prefer that ASBR for forwarding. If you instead used E2, all routers would see the same external metric and distance to the ASBR would not influence selection, potentially causing suboptimal routing. For assessment, configure both ASBRs to export the same prefix, set one to E1 and one to E2, or configure both to E1 and observe which ASBR is preferred on various internal routers based on their OSPF path cost. A reflective task: describe a situation where E2 is preferable — for example when the external metric itself should determine preference irrespective of internal topology. This exercise reinforces how metric-type impacts real-world path selection.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Design Decision
Assessment

Which external type achieves nearest-ASBR preference?

If you want internal routers to choose the nearest ASBR by internal OSPF cost, configure redistributed routes as External Type 1. E1 adds the internal cost to reach the ASBR to the external seed metric so closer routers prefer the closer ASBR.

Assessment task

Create two ASBRs redistributing the same prefix. Configure both to export the prefix as E1 and check which ASBR each internal router prefers based on their OSPF cost.

Reflective question

When might E2 be the better choice? Consider cases where the external seed metric should determine preference regardless of internal topology.

Key Takeaway

Metric-type is a design decision: choose E1 for nearest-ASBR selection; choose E2 when the seed metric alone should determine preference.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Summarizing the essentials: ASBRs are the OSPF mechanism for bringing external prefixes into the domain and they do so by generating external LSAs. Type 5 LSAs are used for general external redistribution and are flooded through the autonomous system except where blocked; Type 7 LSAs are used inside NSSAs and require ABR translation to Type 5 for backbone visibility. The external metric type you choose — E1 or E2 — changes whether internal OSPF cost to the ASBR is added to the advertised seed metric. Use E1 when you want OSPF to prefer the closest ASBR; use E2 when the external seed metric should dominate choice. Lastly, always control redistribution with precise routing-policies and prevent loops with route tagging and filters. These three concepts — ASBR function, LSA type behavior, and metric-type decision — are the core ideas to carry forward into configuration and verification tasks.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will learn what an Autonomous System Boundary Router, or ASBR, does in an OSPF network and why correct redistribution matters. An ASBR is the gateway that imports routes learned by static configuration, other IGPs, or BGP into an OSPF autonomous system. You will learn the LSA mechanisms used to carry those routes — the Type 5 external LSA and the Type 7 NSSA external LSA — and how Junos controls metric and metric-type when redistributing. We will show concrete Junos configuration examples for creating a redistribution policy and applying it to OSPF, including how to set the seed metric and choose between E1 and E2. You will also see practical caveats: stub areas cannot contain an ASBR, NSSAs use Type 7 with ABR translation, and redistribution loops are a common misconfiguration if tagging or filters are not used. By the end you will be able to explain when to prefer E1 versus E2, create a Junos export policy for static routes, and verify external LSAs and learned external routes on internal routers.

These objectives map directly to the practical tasks an engineer will perform when working with ASBRs and external routes. First, you will be able to identify the role and characteristics of an ASBR and explain why it is required to import non-OSPF networks into an OSPF autonomous system. Second, you will understand route redistribution mechanics: how Junos selects routes via a policy, how exported routes are converted into LSAs, and the commands used for verification. Third, you will learn to distinguish between Type 5 and Type 7 LSAs and explain how an NSSA ABR translates Type 7 into Type 5 for backbone distribution. Finally, you will be able to choose and configure external route types, E1 or E2, based on whether internal OSPF cost should influence path selection, and apply that choice in a Junos export statement. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you know when you are ready to practice in a lab or on real devices.

This second objectives slide focuses on actionable skills you will practice. You will create Junos routing-policy statements to select which static or external routes to redistribute, and apply that policy with an OSPF export statement specifying metric and metric-type. You will verify the presence of external LSAs and the external route entry on internal routers using the show ospf database external and show route protocol ospf commands respectively. You will also practice recognizing and preventing redistribution mistakes such as missing filters, incorrect metric-type choices, and the potential for redistribution loops. Finally, you will exercise NSSA-specific behavior: create an ASBR inside an NSSA, observe Type 7 LSAs being generated, and confirm the ABR translates them into Type 5 when propagating into Area 0. These skills let you control reachability and path selection across a production OSPF domain.

An ASBR is a router that connects an OSPF autonomous system to networks outside OSPF and injects those external routes into the OSPF domain. Think of the ASBR as a customs gate between two countries: it informs the OSPF world about routes that exist outside, and it marks information so internal routers can reach those networks. Concretely, an ASBR might redistribute static routes, routes learned from BGP, or routes from another IGP. Without an ASBR performing redistribution, internal OSPF routers would remain unaware of external prefixes. A common real example is a network edge router that learns internet prefixes via BGP and redistributes selected prefixes into OSPF so internal routers can forward traffic to the edge. A common misconception is believing any router connected to an external network becomes an ASBR automatically; in practice the router is only an ASBR when you configure redistribution into OSPF. Another pitfall is placing an ASBR inside a stub or totally stubby area; that violates OSPF rules because those area types block Type 5 LSAs which advertise external routes. Key takeaway: ASBRs enable reachability to external networks by converting non-OSPF routes into OSPF external LSAs, and correct policy and placement are essential to avoid unexpected reachability or LSA filtering issues.

When an ASBR redistributes an external network into OSPF it must advertise that network in a Link-State Advertisement designed for external prefixes. The standard LSA for redistributed routes is the Type 5 External LSA. A Type 5 LSA describes a single external prefix and the originating ASBR; Type 5 LSAs are flooded to all areas in the autonomous system that accept them, except stub and totally stubby areas which block Type 5. A special case exists for Not-So-Totally Stubby Areas: ASBRs inside an NSSA generate Type 7 NSSA External LSAs. Those Type 7 LSAs are flooded only within the NSSA. When a Type 7 reaches the NSSA's ABR, the ABR translates it into a Type 5 LSA so the backbone and other areas can learn the external prefix. This translation supports the NSSA design goal: allow limited external injection while still preventing Type 5s from flooding into the NSSA from outside. A common misconception is that Type 7 LSAs alone reach the backbone; in reality the ABR must perform translation for external knowledge to leave the NSSA. Remember to verify with show ospf database external and show ospf database nssa to confirm which LSA types are present.

Choosing between External Type 2 and External Type 1 routes changes how OSPF evaluates the cost to reach an external destination. E2 is the default for redistributed routes. With E2, routers use the external seed metric advertised by the ASBR; they do not add the internal OSPF cost to reach the ASBR. The practical consequence is that all routers see the same total cost to reach that external destination, so internal topology distance does not change selection. E2 is useful when the advertised external metric alone reflects the desired preference, or when a consistent cost across the domain is acceptable. By contrast, E1 adds the internal OSPF cost to the ASBR to the external seed metric. This means routers closer to an ASBR will see a lower total cost and may prefer that ASBR when multiple ASBRs advertise the same prefix. E1 is appropriate when you want true shortest-path routing to external destinations based on internal topology. A common mistake is leaving metric-type at the default E2 when multiple ASBRs exist, which can result in non-optimal forwarding. Always consider whether internal cost should influence ASBR selection before choosing the metric type.

Let's walk through a Junos configuration pattern to redistribute static routes into OSPF with a controlled metric and metric-type. First, create a policy-statement that matches protocol static and accepts those routes. This policy acts as the filter determining exactly which routes are eligible for export. Next, apply that policy to OSPF with an export statement; you can set metric and metric-type there or within the policy depending on your design. In the provided example we use a policy named REDISTRIBUTE_STATIC and then apply it with set protocols ospf export REDISTRIBUTE_STATIC and set protocols ospf export REDISTRIBUTE_STATIC metric 200 metric-type 1 for E1 behavior. A concrete example: configure a static route for 172.16.10.0/24 on the ASBR, write the policy to match static, and export with metric-type 1 so internal cost is added. A common mistake is forgetting the export statement after creating the policy — the policy exists but isn't applied, so no routes are redistributed. Another pitfall is setting an inappropriate seed metric; choose values consistently across ASBRs when you want predictable comparisons. After configuration, verify with show ospf database external on the ASBR and show route protocol ospf on an internal router to confirm type and metric.

When configuring redistribution on an ASBR follow a clear workflow to avoid mistakes. Step one: identify and verify the external routes you intend to redistribute, for example a static route or routes learned from BGP. Step two: author a routing-policy that precisely matches only those routes; avoid overly broad terms that pick up unintended prefixes. Step three: apply the policy to OSPF with an export statement and choose metric and metric-type according to design — metric-type 2 if seed metric should dominate, metric-type 1 if internal cost should influence selection. Step four: verify on the ASBR that the appropriate external LSAs are generated using show ospf database external or show ospf database nssa for NSSA scenarios. Step five: check internal routers with show route protocol ospf to confirm the external route exists and the metric and type match expectations. Finally, step six: monitor for redistribution loops and unexpected reachability changes; if you redistribute bi-directionally, use route tagging and filters to prevent re-injection into the source protocol. Following this process helps ensure predictable, safe redistribution. Step-by-step Redistribution Workflow means identify → policy → export with metric/metric-type → verify lsas → verify internal routes → prevent loops with tags/filters.. In practical terms, from matching routes to verification on internal routers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

An NSSA allows limited external route injection while preventing Type 5 LSAs from entering the area from outside. When an ASBR inside an NSSA redistributes an external prefix, it generates a Type 7 LSA which is flooded only within the NSSA. The crucial role of the Area Border Router here is translation. When the ABR receives a Type 7 LSA from the NSSA, it converts that LSA into a Type 5 External LSA for distribution into Area 0 and the rest of the autonomous system. This ensures the external route becomes visible to internal routers outside the NSSA while preserving the NSSA's filtering on incoming Type 5 LSAs. Verification steps include checking the ABR's database for both Type 7 and translated Type 5 LSAs. A potential misconception is assuming translation loses the seed metric or type; the ABR preserves the external metric and the chosen metric-type semantics when translating. When designing networks, remember NSSA is useful when you need a local ASBR but do not want Type 5 LSAs to flood into that area; ABR translation bridges local injection with global visibility in a controlled way.

We'll step through the chapter's hands-on scenario: R1 acts as the ASBR connected to Area 0, and R2 is an internal router in Area 0. On R1 create an interface in Area 0, configure a loopback for router ID if needed, and add a static route for the fictitious external network 172.16.10.0/24 with a next-hop. Then create a policy-statement named REDISTRIBUTE_STATIC matching protocol static and accept those routes. Apply the policy to OSPF using set protocols ospf export REDISTRIBUTE_STATIC and set a metric and metric-type; for the exercise the example uses metric 200 metric-type 1 to produce an E1 external route. After committing, verify on R1 with show ospf neighbor to ensure adjacencies, show route 172.16.10.0/24 to confirm the static exists, and show ospf database external to find the Type 5 LSA. On R2 run show route protocol ospf to see 172.16.10.0/24 learned as an external route with type Ext1 and the expected metric of 200 plus internal cost if applicable. If you change metric-type to 2 and re-export, R2 should see the route as Ext2 with the advertised seed metric only. This stepwise exercise reinforces the relationship between policy, export, metric-type, and how OSPF internal routers observe external routes.

While redistribution is powerful, several common mistakes can cause outages or suboptimal routing. First, an incorrect routing-policy may either leak unintended routes into OSPF or fail to export routes you need. Always test policies locally before applying to production. Second, selecting the wrong metric or metric-type can lead to poor path selection. For example, leaving default E2 in a multi-ASBR environment can cause routers to ignore internal distance and choose suboptimal forwarding paths. Third, redistribution loops occur when routes are redistributed in both directions without tagging or filtering; route tags prevent re-injection into the source protocol and are essential in complex designs. Fourth, placing an ASBR inside a stub or totally stubby area violates OSPF rules because these areas block Type 5 LSAs; an NSSA is the correct choice if you need a local ASBR. Finally, forgetting to apply the export statement after creating a policy is a simple but frequent operational error. Use the verification commands described earlier to confirm LSA types and routing table entries to catch these mistakes early. Avoiding Redistribution Pitfalls means use precise policies, choose metric-type intentionally, tag routes to avoid loops, and place asbrs only where lsas are accepted or use nssa appropriately.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Verification is essential after configuring redistribution. Start on the ASBR by confirming OSPF adjacencies with show ospf neighbor; if adjacencies are missing, external LSAs will not propagate correctly. Next, confirm the static or external route is present in the routing table with show route and the specific prefix. Then inspect the OSPF database on the ASBR with show ospf database external to find Type 5 LSAs, or show ospf database nssa to see Type 7 LSAs if working inside an NSSA. On the ABR verify the translation by checking for translated Type 5 entries. Finally, on an internal router run show route protocol ospf; you should see the redistributed prefix with a protocol of OSPF and an external type of Ext1 or Ext2 matching your configuration. If metrics are unexpected, re-check the metric/metric-type on the export statement or the policy. These verification steps let you confirm both LSA generation and the behavior seen by downstream routers. A quick test after changes helps catch policy misconfigurations or unintended route leaks before they affect production traffic. Consider a network where two ASBRs redistribute the same external prefixes into Area 0. The design requirement is that internal routers should prefer the ASBR that is topologically closest in OSPF cost. Which external type should you configure and why? The correct design choice is External Type 1 because E1 adds the internal OSPF cost to the ASBR to the external seed metric. This allows routers nearer to a particular ASBR to see a lower total cost and prefer that ASBR for forwarding. If you instead used E2, all routers would see the same external metric and distance to the ASBR would not influence selection, potentially causing suboptimal routing. For assessment, configure both ASBRs to export the same prefix, set one to E1 and one to E2, or configure both to E1 and observe which ASBR is preferred on various internal routers based on their OSPF path cost. A reflective task: describe a situation where E2 is preferable — for example when the external metric itself should determine preference irrespective of internal topology. This exercise reinforces how metric-type impacts real-world path selection.

Summarizing the essentials: ASBRs are the OSPF mechanism for bringing external prefixes into the domain and they do so by generating external LSAs. Type 5 LSAs are used for general external redistribution and are flooded through the autonomous system except where blocked; Type 7 LSAs are used inside NSSAs and require ABR translation to Type 5 for backbone visibility. The external metric type you choose — E1 or E2 — changes whether internal OSPF cost to the ASBR is added to the advertised seed metric. Use E1 when you want OSPF to prefer the closest ASBR; use E2 when the external seed metric should dominate choice. Lastly, always control redistribution with precise routing-policies and prevent loops with route tagging and filters. These three concepts — ASBR function, LSA type behavior, and metric-type decision — are the core ideas to carry forward into configuration and verification tasks.

Keep these three operational reminders in mind: First, always use a precise routing-policy when redistributing. That policy controls which external prefixes are injected into OSPF and prevents accidental leaks. Second, pick metric-type intentionally: E2 is the default seed-metric-only behavior, while E1 lets internal cost influence ASBR choice and is appropriate in multi-ASBR environments. Third, verify LSA types: use show ospf database external for Type 5 and show ospf database nssa for Type 7 and confirm ABR translation. These reminders help you design predictable redistribution, avoid loops with route tagging, and confirm behavior quickly in a lab or production environment.
